words: statistical question; numerical data; categorical data; distribution; symmetric; skewed; bimodal; uniform
cross_subject: science:HS-LS2-2 (biology compares survey data shown in plots)
notes: Represent one numerical variable with dot plots, histograms and box plots, choose the display that fits the question, and describe the distribution by shape (symmetric, skewed left or right, bimodal, uniform). The course opens with class survey data and published data; students sort statistical from non-statistical questions and numerical from categorical data. Growth from grades 6 and 7: the same three displays, now chosen on purpose and read for shape before any number is computed. Numbers: real data sets of about 10 to 100 values, technology for the larger ones. Limits: one variable at a time; shape words only, no density curves (normal distributions wait for grade 11). IM Alg1.1 lessons 1 to 5 (and 6 to 8 for spreadsheet work). Progressions: shape, centre and spread from 6 to 8 deepened (pdf 283 (p 277)). Modeling: every Statistics and Probability standard is a modeling standard (pdf 282 (p 276)), so data work recurs in grades 10 and 11. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: mean; median; interquartile range; standard deviation; outlier; resistant; spread
cross_subject: science:HS-LS2-2 (comparing centre and spread of two survey data sets)
notes: Compare two or more data sets by centre (mean, median) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation), choosing the pair that suits the shape: median and IQR for skewed data or data with outliers, mean and standard deviation for roughly symmetric data. Students see how one extreme value moves the mean and standard deviation but barely moves the median and IQR, and test outliers with the 1.5 times IQR rule. Standard deviation is computed with technology and read as a typical distance from the mean (grade 6 mean absolute deviation is the bridge). Numbers: real data, decimals to a sensible place. Limits: no hand computation of standard deviation beyond one small worked case; no areas under a normal curve (grade 11). Revisited, not re-owned, in grade 11 (Alg2.7 lessons 4 to 5). IM Alg1.1 lessons 9 to 16. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: quantity; variable; constraint; equation; expression; solution; viable
notes: Read a situation, name the quantities that matter (with units), and write expressions, equations and simple constraints that describe it; check whether a pair of values is a solution and whether it makes sense in the context. The linear unit opens by reasoning about what the letters stand for before any solving. Numbers: whole numbers, decimals and simple fractions from money, time and distance contexts. Representations: words, expressions, equations, tables of value pairs, graphs with labelled axes and scales. Limits: linear relationships in one and two variables only. Starts A-CED.A.2 (owned in grade 11, alg2-rational-functions, where equations reach polynomial and rational relationships), A-CED.A.3 (owned in this grade by alg1-inequalities-two-variables) and N-Q.A.2 (owned in grade 10, geo-solving-right-triangles). IM Alg1.2 lessons 1 to 3. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-CED.A, N-Q.A. Modeling recurs through every algebra unit (Progressions, Algebra, pdf 276 (p 270)).

words: equivalent equations; solution; inequality; solution set; coefficient; justify
notes: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations whose coefficients are letters (solve ax + b = c for x), and explain each step as producing an equivalent equation with the same solutions. Grade 8 multi-step linear equations grow into equations as reasoning: students say why a move is allowed (both sides stay equal) and spot moves that are not. Inequality solutions are graphed on the number line and checked with test values; reversing the inequality when multiplying by a negative is shown with numbers first. Numbers: rational coefficients and letter coefficients. Limits: linear only. A-REI.A.1 (explaining steps) and A-CED.A.1 (creating one-variable equations) are completed in grade 11 with rational equations (alg2-rational-equations). IM Alg1.2 lessons 4 to 7 and 19 to 20. Progressions: solving as a process of reasoning (pdf 279 (p 273)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.A, A-REI.B, A-CED.A. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: formula; solve for; rearrange; literal equation; quantity of interest
notes: Rearrange a formula or a two-variable linear equation to highlight a chosen quantity, using the same moves as in solving equations: d = rt for t, P = 2l + 2w for w, ax + by = c for y (to graph from slope-intercept form). Students check a rearrangement by substituting the same numbers into both forms. Numbers: formulas from geometry, science and money. Limits: the quantity being isolated appears to the first power, or once squared (A = s squared); formulas with the quantity in a denominator wait for grade 11. IM Alg1.2 lessons 8 to 11 and Alg1.4 lesson 16. Applied again in grade 10 for line equations (geo-slope-criteria-lines) and the Pythagorean Theorem (Geo.3 lesson 14), and in grade 11 for rational formulas (Alg2.2 lesson 16). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-CED.A.

words: graph; solution; intercept; slope-intercept form; standard form; ordered pair
notes: Understand that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions: every point on the line makes the equation true and every pair that makes it true is on the line. Students graph linear equations in standard form (Ax + By = C, from the intercepts) and slope-intercept form, move between the forms, and read slope and intercepts in context. Numbers: integer and simple fraction slopes, contexts with money and quantities. Limits: lines here; curves (parabolas, exponentials) reuse the same idea later in the year (alg1-quadratic-equations-reasoning). IM Alg1.2 lessons 5, 10 and 11. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.D.

words: system of equations; solution of a system; substitution; elimination; intersection; no solution; infinitely many solutions
notes: Solve pairs of linear equations in two variables by graphing, substitution and elimination, and prove why elimination works: replacing one equation by its sum with a multiple of the other gives a system with the same solutions. Students choose the method that fits the form, interpret the solution in context, and recognise systems with no solution or infinitely many. Grade 8 systems (mostly by graph and inspection) gain the justification. Numbers: integer and decimal coefficients from contexts. Limits: two linear equations in two variables (the standard says pairs); three-variable systems and matrices are not taught. IM Alg1.2 lessons 12 to 17. Progressions: systems start from the reasoning behind the techniques (pdf 280 (p 274)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.C.

words: linear inequality; half-plane; boundary line; dashed; solid; solution region; constraint; viable
notes: Graph the solutions of a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (dashed boundary for a strict inequality, solid otherwise) and the solutions of a system of linear inequalities as the overlap of half-planes. Students write constraints from contexts (budgets, recipes, time limits), test a point to choose the side, and judge which points in the region are viable in the situation (for example whole numbers of tickets only). Completes A-CED.A.3, started in alg1-writing-equations-constraints. Numbers: integer and decimal coefficients. Limits: linear inequalities only; no optimising an objective function (linear programming is beyond the standard). IM Alg1.2 lessons 21 to 26. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.D, A-CED.A. Modeling: constraints are the modeling use of this skill.

words: two-way table; joint frequency; marginal frequency; relative frequency; conditional relative frequency; association
notes: Summarise two categorical variables in a two-way frequency table, compute joint, marginal and conditional relative frequencies (by row and by column), and use them to say whether the data suggest an association. Grade 8 two-way tables grow into relative frequencies chosen on purpose: which total is the right denominator for the question asked. Numbers: counts up to a few hundred, percents. Limits: association only, no probability language yet (that is grade 10, geo-two-way-probability, which applies this standard again). IM Alg1.3 lessons 1 to 3. Progressions: S-ID.5 (pdf 284 (p 278)).

words: scatter plot; line of best fit; residual; slope; intercept; predict; linear model
notes: Represent two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, fit a line (by eye, then by technology), interpret its slope and intercept in context, and judge the fit by plotting and reading residuals. Students predict with the model and say when a prediction is unreasonable (far outside the data). Grade 8 informal lines of fit become models with units and residuals. Numbers: real data with decimals, rounded to a level the measurements support (N-Q.A.3, owned in grade 10). Limits: linear fits here; fitting exponential and quadratic functions to data (S-ID.B.6a) is started in Alg1.4 and Alg1.5 and completed in grade 11 (alg2-combining-functions-models). IM Alg1.3 lessons 4 to 6. Progressions: least squares line fit by technology (pdf 284 (p 278)). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: correlation coefficient; strong; weak; positive; negative; causation; lurking variable
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (judge whether evidence supports a causal claim)
notes: Compute the correlation coefficient with technology, read it as a measure of how closely the points cluster around a line (near 1 or -1 strong, near 0 weak), and distinguish correlation from causation: a strong association does not show that one variable causes the other, and a third variable can drive both. Students critique causal claims in short reports. Limits: r is interpreted, never computed by hand; causation is argued only from how the data were collected (randomised experiments are grade 11, alg2-study-design-randomness). IM Alg1.3 lessons 7 to 10. Progressions: S-ID.9, a third variable behind both (pdf 286 (p 280)). Numbers: correlation coefficients between -1 and 1 read to two decimal places, from technology. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: function; input; output; domain; range; function notation; evaluate
notes: Understand a function as a rule that assigns each input exactly one output, use function notation f(x), evaluate it, and interpret statements such as f(3) = 12 or f(t) > 50 in context. Students move between descriptions, tables, graphs and equations, and decide whether a relationship is a function. Grade 8 functions gain notation and the words domain and range. Numbers: integers, decimals, simple fractions. Limits: functions of one real variable. Progressions: a function as one quantity determined by another; the vertical line test is not the definition (pdf 240 (p 234), pdf 246 (p 240)). IM Alg1.4 lessons 1 to 5. Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.A. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: intercept; increasing; decreasing; maximum; minimum; average rate of change; interval
notes: Interpret key features of graphs and tables in context (intercepts, where a function increases or decreases, maximums and minimums), sketch a graph from a verbal description, and calculate and interpret the average rate of change over an interval from an equation, a table or (estimated) a graph. Students read solutions of f(x) = g(x) where two graphs meet (A-REI.D.11, completed in grade 11). Numbers: real data and simple expressions. Limits: average rate over an interval only, no instantaneous rate. F-IF.B.4 keeps growing through the quadratic units and is completed in grade 11 with periodicity (alg2-trig-functions-graphs). IM Alg1.4 lessons 6 to 9 and Alg1.5 lesson 10. Progressions: average rate of change for nonlinear functions (pdf 247 (p 241)). Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.B. Modeling standards. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: domain; range; discrete; continuous; reasonable input
notes: Relate the domain of a function to its graph and to the situation it models: whole numbers for counts, nonnegative numbers for time and length, a restricted interval where the context ends. Students describe domain and range in words and with inequalities and decide whether a graph should be separate points or a connected curve. Numbers: integers and decimals. Limits: domains of linear, absolute value, exponential and quadratic functions in this course; excluded values of rational functions are grade 11. IM Alg1.4 lessons 10 to 11, applied in Alg1.5 to 7. Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.B. Modeling standard. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: piecewise function; step function; absolute value; vertex; distance from zero
notes: Graph and interpret piecewise-defined functions (parking and postage rates as step functions) and absolute value functions, reading the absolute value of x as distance from zero and its graph as two linear pieces; shift the absolute value graph up, down, left and right. Numbers: integers and decimals from contexts. Limits: linear pieces only; square root and cube root graphs, the rest of F-IF.C.7b, are completed in grade 10 (geo-scaling-area-volume). F-BF.B.3 is completed in grade 11 (alg2-transformations-functions). IM Alg1.4 lessons 12 to 14. Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.C.

words: inverse function; undo; input; output; swap
notes: Find the inverse of a linear function: describe in words the rule that takes an output back to its input, solve f(x) = c for x, and write the inverse as a function, for example converting temperatures or currencies both ways; interpret the inverse in terms of the quantities. Numbers: integer and decimal coefficients. Limits: linear functions in the base text; the standard's own examples (2 times x cubed, a simple rational function) are not taught there (listed for the lead). Verifying inverses by composition, reading inverses from graphs and restricting domains are (+) and excluded. Applied in grade 10 when cube roots undo cubing (geo-scaling-area-volume). IM Alg1.4 lessons 15 to 17. Progressions: what F-BF.4a expects (pdf 251 (p 245)).

words: linear; exponential; equal differences; equal factors; growth factor; constant rate; percent rate
notes: Distinguish situations modeled by linear functions (equal differences over equal intervals, a constant rate) from those modeled by exponential functions (equal factors over equal intervals, a constant percent rate), prove both properties from tables and equations, and observe from graphs and tables that an increasing exponential eventually overtakes any linear or quadratic function. Numbers: whole-number and decimal growth factors, percents. Limits: whole-number intervals; the comparison with quadratics returns in Alg1.6 lesson 4. Revisited at rational intervals, not re-owned, in grade 11 (alg2-exponential-growth-rational-inputs). IM Alg1.5 lessons 1 to 2 and 19 to 21. Progressions: F-LE.1 (pdf 253 (p 247)). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: exponential growth; exponential decay; growth factor; initial value; negative exponent
notes: Write, graph and interpret exponential functions f(x) = a times b to the x for growth (b > 1) and decay (b between 0 and 1), from a description, a table or two points; read a as the starting value and b as the growth factor; extend to zero and negative integer exponents so the graph runs left of the vertical axis. Contexts: populations, medicine in the body, depreciation. Numbers: whole-number and decimal growth factors; units on both axes. Limits: integer inputs and whole-number time steps; rational inputs, logarithms and base e are grade 11. Starts F-LE.A.2, F-LE.B.5 and F-IF.C.7e (owned in grade 11), F-BF.A.1a (owned in grade 11, alg2-sequences) and N-Q.A.1 (owned in grade 10, geo-modeling-objects-density). IM Alg1.5 lessons 3 to 13. Widely applicable prerequisite: N-Q.A, F-IF.C. Modeling recurs here through the course's modeling prompts. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: percent increase; percent decrease; compound interest; principal; interest rate; compounding period
notes: Write a percent change as a growth factor (a 6 percent increase is times 1.06), build functions for compound interest, compare compounding yearly, monthly and daily, and read an expression such as P(1 + r) to the t as the starting amount times a factor that does not depend on it. Students rewrite an exponential expression to show a different rate and name the percent rate of change in expressions like 0.97 to the t. Grade 7 percent change, often drawn on a tape diagram, becomes a multiplier. Numbers: money to the cent, rates as percents and decimals. Limits: integer exponents; rewriting with rational exponents (1.15 to the power 1/12) is grade 11 (alg2-exponential-growth-rational-inputs), which owns A-SSE.B.3c and F-IF.C.8b; A-SSE.A.1b is owned by alg2-number-e-continuous. IM Alg1.5 lessons 14 to 18. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.A, A-SSE.B, F-IF.C. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: quadratic; second difference; squared term; projectile; area; pattern
notes: Build quadratic functions from growing visual patterns, area situations (rectangles with a fixed perimeter) and falling or thrown objects, and recognise quadratic change in a table (second differences constant), comparing it with linear and exponential change. Students write the expression from the situation and interpret each part. Numbers: integer patterns, decimal heights and times. Limits: quadratics given by the situation; falling-object models use a given coefficient (16 or 4.9) without physics. F-BF.A.1 is completed in grade 11 (alg2-combining-functions-models). IM Alg1.6 lessons 1 to 7. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.A.

words: standard form; factored form; zero; x-intercept; y-intercept; vertex; axis of symmetry; parabola
notes: Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maximums and minimums, and write a quadratic in standard form and factored form to reveal different features: factored form shows the zeros, standard form shows the vertical intercept and, with the sign of the squared term, which way it opens. Students multiply binomials with an area diagram (a rectangle split into four parts) to move from factored to standard form, and see how changing each coefficient moves the graph. Numbers: integer coefficients and zeros first, then fractions and decimals. Limits: real zeros only; factoring with a leading coefficient other than 1 comes in alg1-factoring. IM Alg1.6 lessons 8 to 14. Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.C, A-SSE.A, A-SSE.B. Modeling standard (F-IF.C.7). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: vertex form; vertex; translate; reflect; stretch; parent function
notes: Write and graph quadratics in vertex form a(x - h) squared + k, read the vertex and the direction and width of opening, and predict how changing h, k and a moves, flips or stretches the graph of y = x squared. The grade 8 translation and reflection are reused on a graph. Numbers: integer and simple fraction h, k and a. Limits: from vertex form to a graph here; rewriting standard form into vertex form is alg1-vertex-form-max-min. F-BF.B.3 is completed in grade 11 with all function families and even and odd functions. IM Alg1.6 lessons 15 to 17. Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.C. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: quadratic equation; square root; zero product property; solution; two solutions; no real solution
notes: Write quadratic equations from situations and solve the simplest by reasoning: inspection (x squared = 49), square roots of both sides with both signs, and the zero product property on a factored equation; connect the number of solutions (0, 1 or 2) to where a parabola meets the horizontal axis. Progressions caution: the phrase take the square root of both sides hides the second solution, so solving is taught as reasoning about which numbers make the equation true (pdf 279 (p 273)). Numbers: perfect squares, then square roots left in radical form. Limits: real solutions only; complex solutions are grade 11 (alg2-quadratics-complex-solutions), which owns A-REI.B.4b. IM Alg1.7 lessons 1 to 5. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.B. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: factor; factored form; product; sum; difference of squares; zero of a function
notes: Factor quadratic expressions to reveal the zeros of the function they define and solve equations by factoring: first x squared + bx + c by finding two numbers with product c and sum b (shown in an area diagram), then differences of squares, then leading coefficients other than 1. Students explain why a factored form shows the zeros. Numbers: integer coefficients; leading coefficients other than 1 kept to small integers. Limits: factorable quadratics only; factoring is one method among several (A-REI.B.4b is owned in grade 11). IM Alg1.7 lessons 6 to 10. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.B. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: perfect square; completing the square; equivalent equation; quadratic formula; derive
notes: Recognise perfect square trinomials, complete the square (with an area diagram, then symbols) to rewrite any quadratic equation as (x - p) squared = q with the same solutions, and derive the quadratic formula from that form. Numbers: even then odd linear coefficients, then a leading coefficient other than 1. Limits: real results; when q is negative students say there is no real solution, and complex solutions wait for grade 11. Hands the completing-the-square move to grade 10 circle equations (geo-circle-parabola-equations); the step to complex solutions in grade 11 is listed in the edges file. IM Alg1.7 lessons 11 to 14 and 19. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.B. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: quadratic formula; discriminant; irrational solution; approximate; exact
notes: Use the quadratic formula to solve quadratic equations, including those with irrational solutions; choose among inspection, square roots, factoring, completing the square and the formula by the form of the equation; apply this to contexts such as the height of a launched object. Students give exact (radical) and approximate answers and check them on a graph. Numbers: real coefficients, radicals simplified only as far as needed. Limits: real solutions; the discriminant counts real solutions; complex solutions are grade 11, which owns A-REI.B.4b. IM Alg1.7 lessons 15 to 18. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.B, A-CED.A. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: rational number; irrational number; sum; product; closed; proof
notes: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational, why a rational plus an irrational is irrational, and why a nonzero rational times an irrational is irrational, with algebraic arguments (write each rational as a fraction of integers; argue by contradiction for the irrational cases). Raised by quadratic formula answers: when are the solutions rational? Grade 8 irrational numbers on the number line become a closure argument. Limits: a proof that the square root of 2 is irrational may be shown but is not required. IM Alg1.7 lessons 20 to 21. Progressions: Number, the real number system (pdf 217 to 218 (p 211 to 212)). Widely applicable prerequisite: N-RN.B. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: maximum; minimum; vertex form; complete the square; compare; system
notes: Complete the square in a quadratic expression to write it in vertex form and reveal the maximum or minimum value; use factoring and completing the square to show zeros, extreme values and symmetry and interpret them in context (highest point of a ball, greatest revenue); compare two quadratic functions given in different ways (an equation and a graph: which has the greater maximum). The course closes by solving a simple linear-quadratic system graphically and algebraically (A-REI.C.7 is completed in grade 10 with a line and a circle). Numbers: integer and decimal coefficients from contexts. Limits: quadratics only. IM Alg1.7 lessons 22 to 24 and Alg1.6 lesson 14. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.B, F-IF.C. Modeling: A-SSE.B.3 is a modeling standard.

words: construction; compass; straightedge; circle; radius; perpendicular bisector; angle bisector; inscribed; conjecture
notes: Make formal constructions with compass and straightedge (and paper folding and geometry software): copy a segment and an angle, bisect a segment and an angle, construct perpendicular and parallel lines, and inscribe an equilateral triangle, a square and a regular hexagon in a circle; state precise definitions of segment, angle, circle, perpendicular and parallel lines from the undefined notions point, line, distance along a line and distance around an arc. Students make conjectures from their constructions and give first informal justifications, which become the proofs of later units. Introduces the model construction (compass and straightedge construction as a reasoning tool, a new name because none of the shared names fits), used again for rigid motion definitions, triangle proofs and the circles of a triangle. Limits: constructions are justified, not just performed. IM Geo.1 lessons 1 to 9 and 22. Progressions: Geometry, 7 to 8, high school (pdf 232 (p 226)). Numbers: none computed; lengths and angles are compared by construction, not measured.

words: rigid transformation; translation; rotation; reflection; directed line segment; centre of rotation; line of reflection; image
notes: Describe transformations as functions that take points to points, compare transformations that preserve distance and angle with those that do not (a stretch), define rotations, reflections and translations precisely in terms of angles, circles, perpendicular lines, parallel lines and segments, and draw images and specify sequences of rigid motions that carry one figure onto another. Grade 8 hands-on transformations (tracing paper, the coordinate plane) become definitions students reason from. Representations: tracing paper, constructions, geometry software, coordinates. Limits: rigid motions here; dilations are geo-dilations. IM Geo.1 lessons 10 to 14 and 17 to 18. Progressions: high school builds on grade 8 rigid motions (pdf 221 (p 215)). Numbers: angle measures of rotations in degrees (90, 180, multiples of 60 and 72), coordinates only as a check.

words: symmetry; line of symmetry; rotational symmetry; carries onto; regular polygon
notes: Given a rectangle, parallelogram, trapezoid or regular polygon, describe every rotation and reflection that carries it onto itself, and use symmetry to explain properties (for example why an isosceles trapezoid has congruent base angles). Numbers: angles of rotation as fractions of 360 degrees. Limits: the polygons named in the standard; symmetry of graphs of functions is grade 11 (alg2-transformations-functions). IM Geo.1 lessons 15 to 16.

words: proof; theorem; vertical angles; transversal; alternate interior angles; corresponding angles; perpendicular bisector; equidistant
notes: Prove theorems about lines and angles with rigid motions: vertical angles are congruent; when a transversal crosses parallel lines, alternate interior and corresponding angles are congruent; the points on the perpendicular bisector of a segment are exactly those equidistant from its endpoints. Students write proofs as paragraphs or flow diagrams from conjectures they made with constructions, and prove the triangle angle sum (a start on G-CO.C.10, owned by geo-coordinate-proofs). Limits: proofs rest on the rigid motion definitions and stated assumptions; two-column format is one choice, not the only one. IM Geo.1 lessons 19 to 21 and Geo.2 lessons 8 and 14. Numbers: angle measures in degrees, used in examples before the general proof.

words: congruent; corresponding parts; rigid motion; image; sequence of transformations
notes: Use the definition of congruence (one figure carried onto another by a sequence of rigid motions) to decide whether two figures are congruent and to show that two triangles are congruent exactly when all corresponding sides and angles are congruent. Students name the rigid motions and explain why each part lands on its partner. Grade 8 informal congruence becomes a definition used in proof. Limits: plane figures. IM Geo.2 lessons 1 to 3 and 5. Progressions: G-CO.7 must be proved from the definition (pdf 234 (p 228)). Numbers: none needed; side lengths and angles are named, not measured.

words: side-angle-side; angle-side-angle; side-side-side; criterion; counterexample; isosceles
notes: Explain how the triangle congruence criteria SAS, ASA and SSS follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions, and show with constructions why side-side-angle is not a criterion (two different triangles can fit). Students then use the criteria in proofs, including the isosceles triangle base angles theorem. Limits: the three criteria named in the standard plus the SSA counterexample. IM Geo.2 lessons 4 and 6 to 9 and 11. Progressions: the proof of SSS is more involved (pdf 234 (p 228)). Numbers: side lengths and angles only in counterexamples (two triangles that share SSA but differ).

words: parallelogram; rectangle; rhombus; diagonal; bisect; converse; quadrilateral
notes: Prove theorems about parallelograms: opposite sides are congruent, opposite angles are congruent, the diagonals bisect each other, and conversely; rectangles are parallelograms with congruent diagonals. Students use triangle congruence inside quadrilaterals, test converses, and decide which conditions are enough to name a quadrilateral. Limits: the theorems in the standard; coordinate versions come in geo-coordinate-proofs. IM Geo.2 lessons 10 and 12 to 15. Numbers: none needed; claims are about every parallelogram.

words: dilation; centre of dilation; scale factor; parallel; image; enlarge; reduce
notes: Verify experimentally the properties of a dilation with a given centre and scale factor: a line not through the centre goes to a parallel line, a line through the centre is unchanged, and every segment is scaled by the scale factor. Grade 7 scale drawings and grade 8 dilations on a grid become a transformation with properties students measure and then use. Numbers: whole-number and fraction scale factors. Limits: experimental verification is what the standard asks; proofs that use these properties come next. IM Geo.3 lessons 1 to 4. Progressions: similarity in terms of rigid motions and dilations (pdf 221 (p 215)).

words: similar; similarity transformation; corresponding; proportional; angle-angle; criterion
notes: Use the definition of similarity (a sequence of rigid motions and dilations) to decide whether two figures are similar, explain why similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides, establish the angle-angle criterion, and prove that all circles are similar. Limits: AA is the criterion the standard names; other similarity conditions are explored (Geo.3 lesson 10) but not required. IM Geo.3 lessons 6 to 10. Numbers: scale factors as whole numbers, fractions and decimals.

words: triangle proportionality; side splitter; altitude; Pythagorean Theorem; proportion; similar triangles
notes: Prove that a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally (and the converse), prove the Pythagorean Theorem using similar triangles from the altitude to the hypotenuse, and use congruence and similarity criteria to solve problems and prove relationships in figures (missing lengths, indirect measurement, bank shots). G-SRT.B.5 is applied again in the trigonometry, coordinate and circle units. Numbers: whole numbers, fractions, radicals. IM Geo.3 lessons 5 and 11 to 16. Widely applicable prerequisite: G-SRT.B. Limits: proofs use the similarity criteria and the triangle proportionality theorem; the Pythagorean Theorem is proved by similarity, not by area.

words: sine; cosine; tangent; adjacent; opposite; hypotenuse; acute angle; complementary
notes: Understand that, by similarity, the ratios of sides in a right triangle depend only on its acute angle, which defines sine, cosine and tangent; build a table of ratios for angles, use the 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles as exact cases, and explain why the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement. Numbers: decimal ratios from tables and technology, exact radical ratios for the special triangles. Limits: acute angles in right triangles; the unit circle and angles beyond 90 degrees are grade 11. IM Geo.4 lessons 1 to 6 and 8. Progressions: trigonometric ratios defined from similarity (pdf 236 (p 230)). Widely applicable prerequisite: G-SRT.C.

words: solve a triangle; angle of elevation; inverse trigonometric ratio; approximate; precision
notes: Use trigonometric ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem to solve right triangles in applied problems (ramps, ladders, heights, angles of elevation), find an angle from a ratio with the calculator's inverse functions, define the quantities a model needs, and report answers to a precision the measurements support. Closes by approximating pi from regular polygons inscribed in a circle (a start on G-GMD.A.1). Completes N-Q.A.2 and N-Q.A.3, started in Algebra I. Numbers: decimal measurements, degrees. Limits: right triangles; the laws of sines and cosines are (+) and excluded. IM Geo.4 lessons 7 and 9 to 11. Widely applicable prerequisite: G-SRT.C, N-Q.A. Modeling standard (G-SRT.C.8).

words: cross section; solid of rotation; prism; pyramid; cylinder; cone; sphere; axis
notes: Identify the two-dimensional cross sections of three-dimensional solids (slices of prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones and spheres, parallel and not parallel to the base) and the solids produced by rotating a two-dimensional figure around an axis. Grade 7 slices of right prisms and pyramids grow to any solid and to rotation. Representations: physical models, drawings, geometry software. Limits: identifying and sketching; no cross-section area formulas beyond those in G-GMD.A.1. IM Geo.5 lessons 1 to 3 and 10. Progressions: visualising cross sections (pdf 223 (p 217), pdf 226 (p 220)). Numbers: none computed; shapes are named and sketched.

words: scale factor; area scale factor; volume scale factor; square root; cube root; graph
notes: Scale figures and solids by a factor k and show that areas scale by k squared and volumes by k cubed; work backwards (unscaling) to find the scale factor from a new area or volume, which needs square roots and cube roots; graph square root and cube root functions from these situations. Completes F-IF.C.7b (piecewise and absolute value graphs were Algebra I). Numbers: whole-number and fraction scale factors, decimal roots by technology. Limits: similar figures and solids only. IM Geo.5 lessons 4 to 8 and 18. Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.C, A-SSE.A, A-CED.A. Modeling recurs in this unit's design problems.

words: Cavalieri's principle; volume; prism; cylinder; pyramid; cone; sphere; dissection
notes: Give informal arguments for the circumference and area of a circle and the volumes of cylinders, pyramids and cones (dissection, Cavalieri's principle, cross sections and dilation arguments, informal limits), and use the volume formulas for cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres to solve problems. Grade 7 and 8 volume formulas are explained, not just applied. Numbers: exact answers in terms of pi and decimal approximations. Limits: the sphere formula is given and used without derivation; the Cavalieri argument for the sphere is (+) and excluded. IM Geo.5 lessons 9 to 15. Progressions: G-GMD.1 (pdf 223 (p 217), pdf 238 (p 232)). Modeling standard (G-GMD.A.3).

words: model; density; per unit; design; constraint; estimate; units
notes: Model real objects with geometric shapes (a tree trunk as a cylinder, a person as a set of solids), apply density based on area and volume (people per square mile, mass per cubic centimetre), and solve design problems under physical or cost constraints; use units to guide multi-step work and choose scales on graphs. Completes N-Q.A.1, started in Algebra I. Modeling: these star standards recur in every Geometry unit (the course's modeling prompts and Geo.1 lesson 9, Geo.3 lesson 2, Geo.4 lesson 1, Geo.7 lesson 14), and the row that owns them is the solids unit where IM completes them. Numbers: real measurements, unit conversions. Limits: simplified models stated as such. IM Geo.5 lessons 8 and 16 to 18. Progressions: Quantity, units (pdf 262 (p 256)); Modeling, K to 12 (pdf 300 onward (p 294 onward)). Widely applicable prerequisite: N-Q.A.

words: coordinate rule; mapping; input point; output point; translation rule; reflection rule
notes: Write rigid transformations and dilations as rules on coordinates, (x, y) to (x + 3, y - 2), and use the rules to predict images and to classify a transformation as rigid or not. Applies G-CO.A.2 and G-CO.A.5 (owned by geo-rigid-motion-definitions) and opens analytic geometry. Numbers: integer and fraction coordinates. Limits: rotations by multiples of 90 degrees about the origin; matrix representations are (+) and excluded. IM Geo.6 lessons 1 to 3. Progressions: transformations as functions of points (pdf 241 (p 235)).

words: distance formula; circle equation; centre; radius; parabola; focus; directrix; completing the square
notes: Derive the equation of a circle with given centre and radius from the Pythagorean Theorem (the distance formula), complete the square to find the centre and radius of a circle given in expanded form, and derive the equation of a parabola from a focus and directrix. The Algebra I completing-the-square move is applied to a geometric object. Numbers: integer centres and radii, then fractions and radicals. Limits: circles and parabolas with vertical or horizontal axes; ellipses and hyperbolas are (+) and excluded. IM Geo.6 lessons 4 to 8. Progressions: G-GPE.1 and G-GPE.2 (pdf 237 (p 231)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.B.

words: slope; parallel; perpendicular; opposite reciprocal; point-slope form; intersection
notes: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines (with translations and 90 degree rotations, not by defining parallel through slope), use them to write equations of lines through a point parallel or perpendicular to a given line, and find intersection points of lines with lines and of a line with a circle algebraically and graphically. Completes A-REI.C.7 with the standard's own line-and-circle example, started at the end of Algebra I. Numbers: integer and fraction slopes. Limits: one linear and one quadratic equation in a system. IM Geo.6 lessons 9 to 13. Progressions: avoid circularity in proving the slope criteria (pdf 237 (p 231)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.C, A-CED.A.

words: directed segment; partition; ratio; weighted average; midpoint
notes: Find the point that partitions a directed segment between two given points in a given ratio, first on a number line and then in the plane, and read it as a weighted average of the endpoints (the midpoint is the equal-weight case). Numbers: integer and fraction coordinates, ratios such as 2 to 3. Limits: segments in the plane. IM Geo.6 lessons 15 to 16.

words: coordinate proof; distance formula; midpoint; median; centroid; midsegment; perimeter; area
notes: Use coordinates to prove simple theorems algebraically (that four points form a rectangle or parallelogram, that a point lies on a circle), compute perimeters and areas of polygons from coordinates with the distance formula, and prove the triangle theorems of G-CO.C.10: the angle sum (from Geo.1), the isosceles base angles (from Geo.2), the midsegment parallel to and half the third side, and the medians meeting at one point. Owns G-CO.C.10 here because this unit completes its last two theorems. Numbers: integer coordinates, radicals for lengths. IM Geo.6 lessons 14 and 16 to 17. Modeling standard (G-GPE.B.7). Limits: polygons with vertices given as coordinates or as general letters placed to simplify the algebra.

words: central angle; inscribed angle; chord; arc; tangent; circumscribed angle; diameter
notes: Identify and describe relationships among central, inscribed and circumscribed angles, radii and chords: an inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc, an angle inscribed in a semicircle is right, and a radius is perpendicular to the tangent where it meets the circle. Students prove these with triangle and similarity results. Limits: constructing a tangent from a point outside the circle is (+) and excluded. IM Geo.7 lessons 1 to 3 and 14. Numbers: arc and angle measures in degrees.

words: circumcentre; incentre; inscribed circle; circumscribed circle; cyclic quadrilateral; supplementary
notes: Construct the circumscribed circle of a triangle (perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre) and the inscribed circle (angle bisectors meet at the incentre), and prove that opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle are supplementary. Uses the Geo.1 constructions and the perpendicular bisector theorem. IM Geo.7 lessons 4 to 7. Numbers: none computed. Limits: triangles and cyclic quadrilaterals; the tangent construction from an outside point is (+) and excluded.

words: arc length; sector; central angle; radian; proportional; constant of proportionality
notes: Derive with similarity that the length of an arc cut off by a central angle is proportional to the radius, define the radian measure of the angle as that constant of proportionality (arc length divided by radius), and derive the area of a sector as a fraction of the circle. Introduces the model unit-circle here (a circle of radius 1, where the radian measure equals the arc length) and hands it to the grade 11 trigonometric functions. Numbers: angles in degrees and radians, exact answers in terms of pi. Limits: angles up to one full turn. IM Geo.7 lessons 8 to 13. Progressions: radian measure by similarity, before the unit circle (pdf 255 (p 249)).

words: sample space; outcome; event; subset; union; intersection; complement; and; or; not
notes: Describe events as subsets of a sample space using characteristics of the outcomes, and as unions (or), intersections (and) and complements (not) of other events; list sample spaces with lists, tables and tree diagrams and compute probabilities of equally likely outcomes. Grade 7 chance processes and compound events grow into set language. Numbers: fractions, decimals and percents for probabilities. Limits: finite sample spaces. IM Geo.8 lessons 1 to 3 and 5. Progressions: the shift to conditional probability and independence (pdf 282 (p 276)).

words: two-way table; conditional probability; independent; related events; given
notes: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables when two categories describe each object, use the table as a sample space to estimate conditional probabilities and decide whether events are independent, and explain conditional probability and independence in everyday language (the chance of A given B is not the chance of B given A). Applies the Algebra I relative frequency work (S-ID.B.5). Numbers: counts, relative frequencies as decimals and percents. IM Geo.8 lessons 4, 7 and 9. Progressions: S-CP.4 and S-CP.5 (pdf 294 (p 288)). Limits: two categorical variables, probabilities from relative frequencies in the table.

words: addition rule; or; overlap; mutually exclusive; double counting
notes: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), and interpret the answer in the model, seeing in a table or a Venn-style sketch why the overlap is subtracted once. Numbers: fractions and decimals. Limits: two events. IM Geo.8 lesson 6.

words: conditional probability; independent events; multiplication rule; given; fraction of outcomes
cross_subject: science:HS-LS3-3 (probability of inherited traits in biology)
notes: Find the conditional probability of A given B as the fraction of B's outcomes that also belong to A, understand it as P(A and B) divided by P(B), use P(A and B) = P(A given B) times P(B) in a uniform model, and decide independence by checking whether P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B) or whether P(A given B) = P(A). Contexts: games, medical tests, survey data. Numbers: fractions, decimals, percents. Limits: uniform probability models; permutations, combinations and expected value are (+) and excluded. S-CP.B.8 is a (+) standard owned here because the base text teaches the multiplication rule in this lesson (listed for the lead). IM Geo.8 lessons 8, 10 and 11. Progressions: conditional probability and the rules of probability (pdf 292 (p 286)). Teacher note: medical-test and illness contexts stay general; no student is asked about their own health.

words: sequence; term; arithmetic sequence; geometric sequence; common difference; common ratio; recursive; explicit
notes: Recognise sequences as functions whose domain is a set of integers, sometimes defined recursively (each term from the one before); write arithmetic and geometric sequences both recursively and with an explicit formula, translate between the two, and use them to model situations (a stack of cups, a bouncing ball). Students graph sequences as separate points and see arithmetic sequences as linear and geometric sequences as exponential functions on the integers. Completes F-BF.A.1a (an explicit expression, a recursive process or steps from a context), started in Algebra I. Numbers: integer and fraction differences and ratios; first term indexed from 0 or 1, said each time. Limits: arithmetic, geometric and simple other recursive sequences (Fibonacci shown). IM Alg2.1 lessons 1 to 10. Progressions: sequences are functions (pdf 241 (p 235), pdf 246 (p 240)). Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.A. Modeling standards (F-BF.A.1, F-BF.A.2). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: series; finite geometric series; sum; common ratio; loan payment
notes: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series with ratio not 1 (multiply by the ratio and subtract, or use the identity behind x to the n minus 1) and use it to solve problems such as the total of repeated deposits or a loan or mortgage payment. Numbers: decimal ratios from interest rates, technology for large n. Limits: finite series; infinite series are beyond the standard. IM Alg2.1 lesson 11 and Alg2.2 lessons 23 to 26. Progressions: the identity that founds the series formula (pdf 272 (p 266)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.B. Modeling standard.

words: polynomial; degree; term; coefficient; leading coefficient; closed; standard form
notes: Understand that polynomials form a system like the integers, closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication; add, subtract and multiply polynomials (with an area diagram for products); interpret terms, factors and coefficients in context, such as the volume of an open box cut from a sheet as a cubic polynomial. The Algebra I quadratic is the degree 2 case. Numbers: integer coefficients, then rational. Limits: division is alg2-polynomial-division-remainder; A-SSE.A.1a is owned here because the polynomial unit completes it. IM Alg2.2 lessons 1 to 4. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-APR.A, A-SSE.A.

words: zero; factor; multiplicity; end behaviour; degree; turning point; rough graph
notes: Identify the zeros of a polynomial when a suitable factored form is available, use them (with multiplicity: crossing or touching the axis) and end behaviour (from the degree and leading coefficient) to sketch a rough graph, and write a polynomial with given zeros. Algebra I factored form for quadratics grows to any degree. Numbers: integer and simple fraction zeros. Limits: factorisations given or easy to find; no rational root theorem. IM Alg2.2 lessons 5 to 10. Progressions: constructing polynomials with specified zeros (pdf 274 (p 268)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-APR.B. Modeling standard (F-IF.C.7). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: polynomial division; quotient; remainder; Remainder Theorem; factor
notes: Divide polynomials by linear factors (with a division diagram and with long division), know and apply the Remainder Theorem (the remainder on division by x - a is p(a), so p(a) = 0 exactly when x - a is a factor) and use it to find factors and zeros; find where two polynomial graphs intersect. Numbers: integer coefficients. Limits: division by linear factors; division by higher-degree divisors only as rewriting rational expressions (alg2-rational-functions). IM Alg2.2 lessons 11 to 15. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-APR.B.

words: rational function; vertical asymptote; horizontal asymptote; end behaviour; average cost; undefined
notes: Write rational functions from situations (average cost per item, the side of a box with a fixed volume that minimises surface area), graph them showing zeros, vertical asymptotes where the denominator is zero, and end behaviour, and rewrite a(x)/b(x) as q(x) + r(x)/b(x) by inspection or long division to reveal the end behaviour. Completes A-CED.A.2 (equations in two variables from linear through rational relationships, with labelled axes and scales). F-IF.C.7d is a (+) standard owned here because the base text teaches it in these lessons while naming only F-IF.C.7 (listed for the lead). Numbers: integer coefficients. Limits: simple rational functions with linear or quadratic parts; holes are mentioned, not studied. IM Alg2.2 lessons 16 to 19. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-APR.D, A-CED.A. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: rational equation; solve; justify; equivalent; extraneous solution; check
notes: Create one-variable equations from contexts (including rational and exponential relationships) and solve rational equations, explaining each step as following from the previous one on the assumption that a solution exists, and checking for values that make a denominator zero. Completes A-CED.A.1 and A-REI.A.1, started in Algebra I with linear and quadratic equations. Numbers: integer coefficients. Limits: simple rational equations; solutions also found where graphs meet. IM Alg2.2 lessons 20 to 22. Progressions: solving as reasoning, extraneous solutions (pdf 279 (p 273)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-CED.A, A-REI.A. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: identity; prove; difference of squares; sum of cubes; Pythagorean triple; structure
notes: Prove polynomial identities by expanding and rearranging, and use them to describe numerical relationships (an identity that generates Pythagorean triples, the difference of squares used for mental arithmetic); use the structure of an expression to see a rewrite, such as x to the 4 minus y to the 4 as a difference of squares. Completes A-SSE.A.2, practised in Algebra I factoring. Numbers: integers. Limits: identities provable by algebra; the binomial theorem is (+) and excluded. IM Alg2.2 lessons 23 to 25. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-APR.C, A-SSE.A.

words: rational exponent; radical; square root; cube root; nth root; exponent rules
notes: Explain how the meaning of a rational exponent follows from keeping the properties of integer exponents (5 to the 1/3 is the cube root of 5 because its cube must be 5), and rewrite expressions with radicals and rational exponents using those properties, including negative rational exponents. Students locate values such as 8 to the 2/3 on a number line and on the graph of an exponential function. Numbers: integer bases, unit and non-unit fraction exponents. Limits: real roots; even roots of negatives are left undefined until complex numbers. IM Alg2.3 lessons 1 to 5. Progressions: rational exponents preserve the laws of exponents (pdf 217 to 218 (p 211 to 212)). Widely applicable prerequisite: N-RN.A. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: radical equation; extraneous solution; squaring both sides; inequivalent equations; check
notes: Solve simple square root and cube root equations, and rational equations, and give examples of how an extraneous solution can arise when both sides are squared (the new equation is not equivalent); check solutions in the original equation and on a graph. Completes A-REI.A.2, started with rational equations. Numbers: integers and simple radicals. Limits: one radical per equation in most cases. IM Alg2.3 lessons 6 to 9 and Alg2.2 lesson 22. Progressions: extraneous solutions (pdf 279 (p 273)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.A. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: complex number; imaginary unit; i; real part; imaginary part; a + bi
notes: Know that there is a number i with i squared equal to -1 and that every complex number can be written a + bi with a and b real; add, subtract and multiply complex numbers with the commutative, associative and distributive properties. Students first meet the need: x squared = -1 has no solution on the real number line. Numbers: integer real and imaginary parts. Limits: conjugates, moduli, division and the complex plane are (+) and excluded. IM Alg2.3 lessons 10 to 14. Progressions: complex numbers let every quadratic be solved (pdf 219 (p 213)).

words: complex solution; non-real; discriminant; quadratic formula; a plus or minus bi
notes: Solve quadratic equations with real coefficients that have complex solutions, by completing the square and the quadratic formula; recognise from the discriminant (or a graph that misses the horizontal axis) when the solutions are not real and write them as a plus or minus bi. Completes A-REI.B.4b, practised with real solutions in Algebra I. Numbers: integer coefficients. Limits: real coefficients; extending identities to complex numbers and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra are (+) and excluded. IM Alg2.3 lessons 15 to 19. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.B. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: growth factor; decay; half-life; rational input; equivalent expression; monthly rate; annual rate
notes: Construct exponential functions from a graph, a description or two input-output pairs, now with rational inputs (the growth factor over half a year or a month), rewrite exponential expressions with exponent properties to show a different time unit (1.15 to the t as the 12th root of 1.15 raised to the 12t, about 1.012 to the 12t), name the percent rate of change and classify growth or decay, and use half-life. Completes F-LE.A.2 (including arithmetic and geometric sequences from alg2-sequences), A-SSE.B.3 and its part c, and F-IF.C.8b, all started in Algebra I. Numbers: decimal factors, technology for roots. Limits: base e is alg2-number-e-continuous. IM Alg2.4 lessons 1 to 7. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.B, F-IF.C. Modeling standard (A-SSE.B.3). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: logarithm; base; exponent; log base 10; natural logarithm; solve for the exponent
notes: Express the solution of an exponential equation a times b to the ct = d as a logarithm, with base 2, 10 or e, and evaluate it with technology; read log base 10 of 1000 as the exponent that turns 10 into 1000 and estimate logarithms between known powers. Numbers: bases 2, 10 and e as the standard says. Limits: for most students a logarithm is shorthand for the solution of an exponential equation; logarithms as inverse functions and the laws of logarithms are for advanced courses (Progressions pdf 253 (p 247)), so F-BF.B.5 is excluded. IM Alg2.4 lessons 8 to 11 and 14.

words: e; continuous growth; continuous compounding; parameter; interpret
notes: Meet e as the limit of compounding more and more often, write and interpret exponential models with base e, and interpret every parameter of a linear or exponential function in context (starting value, rate, growth factor); interpret complicated expressions by seeing a part as one quantity (P times e to the rt as the principal times a growth factor). Completes F-LE.B.5, A-SSE.A.1 and A-SSE.A.1b, started in Algebra I. Numbers: decimal rates, technology for e. Limits: no calculus; continuous growth is defined through compounding. IM Alg2.4 lessons 12 to 13. Widely applicable prerequisite: A-SSE.A. Modeling standard (A-SSE.A.1).

words: intersection; graph; logarithmic function; solution; approximate; scale
notes: Explain why the x-coordinates where y = f(x) and y = g(x) meet are the solutions of f(x) = g(x), and find them approximately with graphs, tables or successive approximation for linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential and logarithmic functions; graph logarithmic functions and use them for acidity and earthquake scales. Completes A-REI.D.11, started in Algebra I. Numbers: decimals, technology. Limits: logarithmic graphs read as the solutions of exponential equations, not as inverses (+). IM Alg2.4 lessons 15 to 18 and Alg2.2 lessons 11 and 21. Progressions: equations as intersections of graphs (pdf 241 (p 235)). Widely applicable prerequisite: A-REI.D. Modeling standard.

words: translation; reflection; vertical stretch; horizontal stretch; even function; odd function; symmetry
notes: Identify the effect on a graph of replacing f(x) by f(x) + k, k times f(x), f(kx) and f(x + k) for positive and negative k, find k from two graphs, explain the effects with technology, and recognise even and odd functions from graphs (symmetry in the vertical axis or the origin) and from equations. Grade 10 transformations of the plane return as transformations of graphs, for every family met so far. Numbers: integer and fraction k. Limits: one or two transformations at a time; composition of functions is (+) and excluded. IM Alg2.5 lessons 1 to 9. Progressions: transformations of graphs and equations (pdf 242 (p 236)). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: model; fit; combine functions; sum of functions; data; transformation of a model
notes: Write functions that describe relationships between quantities, combine standard function types with arithmetic (a cooling drink as a constant plus a decaying exponential), and fit a function to data by choosing a family suggested by the context and transforming it to match, then use the model to answer questions in context. Completes F-BF.A.1 and S-ID.B.6a (linear, quadratic and exponential fits), started in Algebra I. Numbers: real data, technology. Limits: given or chosen families; regression beyond technology fits is not required. IM Alg2.5 lessons 10 to 11 (and 1, 3, 7, 8 for fitting). Modeling: F-BF.A.1 is a modeling standard; data modeling recurs from Algebra I units 3 and 5. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: unit circle; radian; terminal side; cosine; sine; coordinates; standard position
notes: Understand radian measure as the length of the arc an angle cuts on the unit circle, and explain how the unit circle extends sine and cosine from acute angles to all real numbers: the cosine and sine of an angle are the coordinates of the point it reaches, counterclockwise from (1, 0), for any number of turns and negative angles. Grade 10 right triangle ratios and radians (geo-arcs-sectors-radians) come together. Numbers: radians as multiples of pi and as decimals. Limits: exact values from the special triangles are found through symmetry of the circle; the (+) work on special angles and odd and even symmetry is excluded. IM Alg2.6 lessons 1 to 4, 7 and 10 to 11. Progressions: extend the domain using the unit circle after right triangle trigonometry (pdf 255 (p 249)).

words: Pythagorean identity; quadrant; sign; sine squared; cosine squared
notes: Prove the Pythagorean identity, sine squared plus cosine squared equals 1, from the unit circle and the Pythagorean Theorem, and use it to find sine, cosine or tangent from one of the others and the quadrant of the angle. Numbers: fractions and radicals. Limits: the identity in the standard; addition formulas are (+) and excluded. IM Alg2.6 lessons 5 to 6. Progressions: F-TF.8 (pdf 258 (p 252)).

words: periodic; period; amplitude; midline; tangent; frequency; trigonometric function
notes: Graph sine, cosine and tangent as functions of a real number, showing period, midline and amplitude, transform them, and interpret key features of any function in context including the last item in the list, periodicity. Completes F-IF.C.7 and F-IF.C.7e (exponential and logarithmic graphs were earlier in this course and in Algebra I) and F-IF.B.4, whose features have grown since Algebra I. Numbers: radians, amplitude and midline values from contexts. Limits: technology for complicated cases, by hand in simple ones. IM Alg2.6 lessons 8 to 9 and 12 to 17. Widely applicable prerequisite: F-IF.B, F-IF.C. Modeling standards. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: model; periodic phenomenon; amplitude; frequency; midline; ferris wheel; tide
cross_subject: science:HS-PS4-1 (waves described by frequency and wavelength)
notes: Choose and write trigonometric functions to model periodic situations with a given amplitude, frequency (or period) and midline: a Ferris wheel seat's height, tides, daylight hours, a point on a wheel. Students check the model against data and say where it fails. Numbers: real measurements and units. Limits: sine and cosine models; solving trigonometric equations with inverse functions is (+) and excluded. Modeling: this star standard recurs in the course's modeling prompts. IM Alg2.6 lessons 13, 16, 18 and 19.

words: population; sample; parameter; statistic; random sample; survey; experiment; observational study; randomisation
notes: Understand statistics as a way to infer population parameters from a random sample, and recognise the purposes of and differences among sample surveys, experiments and observational studies, explaining how randomisation works in each (random selection lets a sample speak for a population; random assignment lets an experiment speak about cause). Builds on Algebra I correlation and causation. Limits: design and reasoning, no formal tests. IM Alg2.7 lessons 1 to 3. Progressions: inference rests on randomisation (pdf 282 (p 276)). Numbers: proportions and means from class surveys, only to illustrate. Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: normal distribution; bell-shaped; standard deviation; percent of data; area under a curve; z-score
notes: Use the mean and standard deviation of a data set to fit it to a normal distribution and estimate population percentages with technology or tables (areas under the curve), and recognise data sets for which a normal model is not appropriate (skewed, bimodal). Algebra I displays and standard deviation are applied to a model curve; area of a histogram's bars links to area under the curve. Numbers: real data, decimals, percents. Limits: estimating areas with technology; no calculus. IM Alg2.7 lessons 4 to 7. Progressions: S-ID.4 (pdf 284 (p 278)). Skips grade 10 on purpose: Geometry carries no algebra or functions unit, so Algebra II builds on Algebra I directly (IM course order Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II).

words: simulation; sampling variability; estimate; proportion; mean; margin of error; model
notes: Decide whether a probability model is consistent with results from a data-generating process by simulation (would 5 tails in a row make you doubt a fair coin?), and use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean or proportion, developing a margin of error from the spread of many simulated samples. Grade 10 probability and Algebra I spread come together. Numbers: proportions and means, technology for simulation. Limits: margin of error from simulation, not from formulas. IM Alg2.7 lessons 8 to 12. Progressions: margins of error through simulation (pdf 288 to 289 (p 282 to 283)).

words: randomised experiment; treatment; control; difference of means; re-randomisation; significant; report
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (evaluate whether a report's evidence supports its claim)
notes: Use data from a randomised experiment to compare two treatments, and use simulation (re-randomising the results many times) to decide whether an observed difference is larger than chance alone would make it; evaluate reports based on data, asking how the data were collected and whether the conclusion follows. Completes the inference unit. Numbers: means and proportions, technology. Limits: simulation-based reasoning, no formal hypothesis tests. IM Alg2.7 lessons 13 to 16 (and 1, 2 and 10 for reports). Progressions: S-IC.5 (pdf 290 (p 284)). Teacher note: experiments about health (heart rates, caffeine) use class-safe activities only; no student shares medical information.
